fixes.explanation: Right, baker! The LORD says Assyria will fall "…not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals." (Isaiah 31:8). So this is a sword that mortals did not make. I think this verse is a heavy one, so I'll just say it plainly. The answer is what the LORD said: not made by mortals.

Horses, baker! Isaiah says they "…rely on horses, who trust in their abundance of chariots and in their multitude of horsemen." (Isaiah 31:1). Hooves, wheels and riders, all piled up. That's a whole lot of trusting, and not one item on the list is the LORD.

I see why you'd think it, but it's the opposite. Isaiah says of them, "…They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD." (Isaiah 31:1). They're looking at the horses and not at Him. It's like telling a friend you're listening while your eyes never leave your phone.

False, and Isaiah says it plainly: "…They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD." (Isaiah 31:1). Their trust sits in the horses, the chariots and the horsemen. The LORD isn't on that list, and the woe is aimed at exactly these people.

Yes! Isaiah says of the LORD, "…He does not call back His words." (Isaiah 31:2). Once He has spoken, it stands. I can't say that about myself. I've called back "I'm only having one cookie" more times than I can count.

Not quite. Isaiah says the opposite: "…He does not call back His words." (Isaiah 31:2). Nothing in the verse has Him swapping them out later. His words stand, and that includes the part about disaster.
Close, but no. Isaiah doesn't mention hiding anything. He says, "…He does not call back His words." (Isaiah 31:2). The point is that He doesn't take them back. What He has said stays said.

Both, baker. Isaiah says "…the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together." (Isaiah 31:3). I think this one is heavy, so I'll say it plainly. The helper doesn't stand off to the side while the other one falls. Just before this, Isaiah says "…the Egyptians are men, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit." (Isaiah 31:3).

Not just the helper. Isaiah says "…the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together." (Isaiah 31:3). The one being helped doesn't walk away. They go down together, and that's a heavy thing to read.

Not only that one. Isaiah says "…the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together." (Isaiah 31:3). The helper doesn't get a pass. Both of them perish together, and I think that's a heavy verse.

True! The LORD says the lion "…is not terrified by their shouting or subdued by their clamor…" (Isaiah 31:4). A whole band of shepherds is called out against it, making all that noise, and it isn't scared. I'd have been halfway to the next county. My mustache would've been a white flag.

Other way around. The lion "…is not terrified by their shouting or subdued by their clamor…" (Isaiah 31:4). The shepherds are called out against it and make plenty of noise. Still, it isn't terrified and it isn't subdued.

Nice thought, but that's not in this verse. The LORD says, "…the LORD of Hosts will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights." (Isaiah 31:4). The lion picture is about a battle, not about building. He comes down to do battle.

Tempting if you like tidy numbers, but no. The LORD says, "…the LORD of Hosts will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights." (Isaiah 31:4). The lion picture is a battle picture. Counting isn't in this verse.

Protect! "Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem. He will shield it and deliver it; He will pass over it and preserve it." (Isaiah 31:5). Those are warm words after all that woe. Shield, deliver, pass over, preserve. That's four promises stacked up.

I get it, after all that woe it might feel that way. But the verse says, "Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem." (Isaiah 31:5). It goes right on to say, "He will shield it and deliver it…" (Isaiah 31:5). Those are words of protecting, not abandoning.

Not this time. The verse says, "Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem." It goes on, "He will shield it and deliver it…" (Isaiah 31:5). Nothing in this picture is a test. The word is protect.

Not gifts. The message says, "Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled, O children of Israel." (Isaiah 31:6). It's the coming back that matters here. Nothing in the call asks anyone to carry anything. It asks them to return.

Idols! The message says, "…every one of you will reject the idols of silver and gold that your own hands have sinfully made." (Isaiah 31:7). The verse says their own hands made them, and it calls that sinful. I think this one is heavy, but it looks ahead to a day when every one of them rejects those idols.

Silver and gold do sound like crown material. But the verse says, "…every one of you will reject the idols of silver and gold that your own hands have sinfully made." (Isaiah 31:7). They're idols, not crowns. The rejecting is for that day, when every one of them will do it.

Egypt comes up earlier in this passage, but not here. The LORD says, "…a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals." (Isaiah 31:8). Since mortals didn't make that sword, a forge in Egypt isn't the answer. Assyria falls "…not by the sword of man…" (Isaiah 31:8).

Good thinking, but the verse doesn't point to anyone's army. The LORD says Assyria will fall "…not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals." (Isaiah 31:8). Judah's army isn't named in the verse. The answer has to match what the verse says about the sword.

Not this time. The LORD says, "…They will flee before the sword, and their young men will be put to forced labor." (Isaiah 31:8). Assyria flees instead of holding its ground. That's the opposite of standing and fighting it out.

False, baker. The LORD says, "…They will flee before the sword, and their young men will be put to forced labor." (Isaiah 31:8). They flee, so they don't stand their ground. I think this verse is a heavy one, with the forced labor in it.

Yes! "…their princes will panic at the sight of the battle standard," declares the LORD (Isaiah 31:9). The sight of it is what sets them off. It's like your boss's name popping up on your phone at 9 at night. Nobody's said a word yet, and your stomach already dropped.
